extracted.intended_audience: trainees and practitioners writing grant proposals for adult basic education guidance/counseling (adult education counselors, program staff, grant writers in adult education)
extracted.subtask_short: writing funding proposals for adult education
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional guidance and checklists for drafting, formatting, and self-evaluating funding proposals for adult basic education guidance/counseling projects, including research designs, budgets, evaluation plans, and presentation. Geared toward trainees who will produce sample proposals for submission to funding agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral objective components
rubrics_metrics.description: A behavioral objective should have the following components: (I.a) A statement of a specific task (observable, measurable behavior). (I.b) Who is doing the task. (II) A statement of conditions for arriving at competence (how the task is to be accomplished). (III) A statement of criteria which provides a standard of competence against which desired outcomes (task) can be measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: include task, who, conditions, criteria in each objective; e.g., 'The trainee will be able to write a behavioral objective, as a result of participating in a three-hour workshop. Evidence will be determined when the trainee accurately rewrites eight out of ten inadequately stated objectives including task, conditions, and criteria.' Use observable/measurable verbs. Objectives should include task, conditions, and criteria and be defendable to a supervisor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research proposal required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A research proposal should include: 1) a clear problem statement, 2) unambiguous hypotheses, 3) operational definitions, and 4) clearly stated research methodology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preassessment requires submission of a proposal with these elements. Readings and references (Kerlinger, Van Dalen, Campbell, etc.) suggested. Incorporate experimental/quasi-experimental designs, define dependent/independent variables, pretest/posttest, control/experimental groups where appropriate. Include explicit operational definitions and hypotheses tied to measurable outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure of the project (detailed requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Procedure section should describe in detail the steps to be followed and, where pertinent, include: (a) populations, samples, experimental and control groups (origin, composition, numbers, types of data, sampling plans), (b) experimental design and methods, (c) data types to be gathered and instruments (questionnaires, interview guides, tests, unpublished instruments), (d) analyses—methods of statistical and other analyses to test hypotheses or answer objectives, (e) approximate time schedule for phases of the project, (f) expected end-product (including a final report).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This section provides the primary basis for evaluating the proposal—be specific. Describe measurement instruments, sampling, and analysis methods in enough detail that a reviewer understands how objectives will be tested. Flow-charting and time sequencing are recommended. If activity costs are relevant, tie them to procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of the problem and need
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement should be clear yet brief, with definite conclusions drawn and the significance of the problem specifically indicated. Include who the target groups are and the effects on them; why the problems are not presently being met; plan for incorporation after outside funding ends; professional and lay groups involved; brief review of related projects; and anticipated outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a sense of urgency; avoid ambiguous terms—clarify in operational terms. Introduce the approach as a preview of the proposal. Demonstrate insight and knowledge in the area so reviewers believe you can deliver. Use staff/lay involvement, review & research, identification of needs, priority listing leading to problem statements and expected outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives of the project (qualities and types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectives should be stated concisely, be quantifiable (measurable), realistic (doable), limited in number (don't have too many), and be separable from procedures. Types include covert (avoid self-serving) and overt. Objectives may be general (goals) or specific (measurable objectives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure objectives flow from problem statements and relate directly to needs. Use measurable verbs (see 'verb usage' guidance). List objectives in order of importance. Match objectives to funding agency philosophy and, when possible, incorporate language used by the funder. Include sample enabling objectives in an off-file if many are needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation design (components and expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation should address antecedent (input), transaction (implementation process), outcomes (product), and outcome differential (difference between outcome and antecedent). Every objective should be paralleled by description of measures to indicate attainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe methods of evaluation, timeline, who will evaluate, how data will be handled/stored, dissemination plans, sampling techniques, auditing procedures if required, and whether outcomes can be replicated. Distinguish institutional inventory, operational (formative) evaluation, and final (summative) evaluation. Include both objective and subjective data and specify analyses to be used to test hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget: required content and cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Budgets should contain an organizational chart, specific staff requirements, job descriptions, resumes (if personnel known), salaries and fringe benefits, equipment needed, consumable supplies, travel requirements with specifics (miles, modes, persons), miscellaneous expenses, sources and amounts of funds including in-kind contributions, and indirect costs. If multi-year, indicate separate years in separate columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List all position titles, percent of time on project, and per annum salaries including retirement/Social Security. Itemize operating expenses (materials, statistical services, duplicating, office supplies). Do not overbudget—ask for what you actually need. Indicate other support and whether proposal has been submitted elsewhere and if it's an extension to a prior project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and organization of the proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical format includes three categories: I. The Preliminaries (title page, table of contents, list of tables/figures), II. The Text of the Proposal (Introduction—Statement of the Problem, Identification of Need, Justification, Related Research, Objectives, Procedures, Work Plan, Sequence of Activities, Evaluation), III. Reference Materials (appendices, agency forms, project abstract, budget, personnel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow pagination rules (Roman numerals for preliminaries, Arabic for text; initial pages of major subdivisions are counted but may not display numerals). Each chapter/major subdivision should begin on a new page. Use consistent heading/subheading conventions (centered head, free-standing sidehead, paragraph sidehead) and only use subheadings when functional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and form / presentation quality
rubrics_metrics.description: First impressions are critical. Reviewers appraise general appearance, neatness, charts, maps, graphs, list of figures, table of contents, title page, consistency of style, completeness, and professionalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish final drafts: check typing, proofreading, graphics. Consider hiring an artist for cover or charts if needed. Adopt and follow a consistent typing/style manual. Ensure final copy is neat and clean; sloppy typing or art work can cost you the proposal. Use clear, concise language and avoid jargon and pomposity (see Appendix B humorous guidance: 'DON'T USE BIG WORDS!').

rubrics_metrics.name: Title rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The title should be brief but accurate and comprehensive, ideally composed of three or four words or groups of words and should accurately limit the subject under discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include words or phrases that someone would search for to find information about the subject. Avoid grandiose or awkward titles. Make the meaning clear on first reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table of contents and list of tables/figures formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Table of Contents lists chapter/section headings and main subdivisions with page citations and must correspond exactly in wording with headings in the text. Main headings are in full capitals and consecutively numbered in Roman caps; subheadings use initial capitals only for first word/proper nouns. Lists of tables/figures show captions/titles and page numbers; tables numbered with capital Roman numerals, figures with Arabic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate indentation to show relationships. Double-space all lines. Use leaders to guide the eye to right-aligned page numbers. If a heading wraps, indent subsequent lines two spaces from first letter. No terminal punctuation for headings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal review/self-evaluation checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: A checklist for the writer to self-evaluate a proposal prior to submission includes general checks (fit within grantor's guidelines, evaluation procedures considered, continuity between sections, specificity, style and form, etc.) and section-specific checks for Statement of the Problem, Related Research, Objectives, Procedure, and other elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Yes/No answers to ensure completeness. Example items: 'Is the statement convincing? Is the problem clearly defined? Have you reviewed recent data? Are objectives testable? Is the sequence of steps clear? Have you included copies of tests/instruments?' If answers indicate gaps, further development is needed before submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief investigator proposal checklist (responsibilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsibility checklist items include: Have all potential sponsors been considered? Have budgetary considerations been cleared with appropriate offices? If reimbursed time is involved, has it been cleared? Have institutional equipment uses been budgeted? Has provision been made for indirect allowance? Have sufficient copies been prepared? Are required signatures on finished copies? Does the proposal give a realistic presentation of needs? Does it fulfill sponsor requirements/specifications?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circle appropriate data (Yes/No) and provide comments. Ensure administrative approvals and clearance of budget/personnel issues before submission. Confirm signatures and number of signed copies required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendices and reference materials inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference materials and appendices should follow the text and may include agency forms, project abstract, budget, budget justification, personnel, list of figures, and any additional supporting documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendices are preceded by a division sheet marked APPENDIX. Include tests, instruments, questionnaires, unpublished measures, resumes, and any documentation referenced in the proposal. Use appendices to house material that reviewers may need but which would disrupt the main narrative if included inline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management design and flowcharting
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a network-based flow diagram for project management showing the sequence of events (e.g., project funded → director selected → staff selected → workshops → curriculum selection → baseline data collection → termination). Circles represent completed events; lines represent activities leading to events. Add estimated times to indicate durations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flowcharting is derived from procedures and evaluation design. Use it to plan staffing, consultant criteria, selection processes, and timelines. Itemize budgeting for resources and facilities needed. A coherent flowchart demonstrates project feasibility and management competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auditing (when applicable)
rubrics_metrics.description: If auditing is called for, delineate auditing procedures and include auditing costs in the budget. Auditing can (a) duplicate evaluation procedures, (b) operate a different evaluation system then compare results, (c) focus on the evaluation system itself, or (d) combine any of these functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auditing functions as an external quality-control agent and may be sensitive—handle carefully. Consider potential threats to institutions, skepticism about auditing techniques, and auditor qualifications. Use auditing as validation of evaluation when appropriate and required by funder guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance objectives: definition and acceptance criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance is the observable behavioral actions of individuals/groups. An objective is a time-limited target with definable parameters. A well-written objective should say: (1) what learners will be able to do, (2) under what conditions, and (3) to what extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectives should: describe learner behaviors demonstrating achievement; specify important conditions under which competence is demonstrated; delineate standards for judging proficiency; use action words that preclude misinterpretation; be detailed enough to recognize expected outcomes; and contain a justification/validation of the expected outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures: specific questions to answer
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures should explicitly answer: (1) What are you going to do? (2) Who or what is involved? (3) How are you going to do it? (4) What will the end product be? (5) What is the time schedule for each activity? (6) How will you analyze the results?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific and detailed. Include sequence/steps, flow charts, time frames, external political processes, evaluation steps, expected products, and contribution. Show coherence between problem, objectives, and procedures. Where alternatives were considered, show reasons for selecting the final procedure.
